title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: In an agent, what decides which step comes next?

options.text: The programmer's code, which fixes the order of steps in advance
The user, who approves each step before the next one runs
The model, which chooses its next action from the results so far
The tool, which tells the program what should be called next

items.stem: Every booking request to your makerspace assistant needs the same four steps in the same order: read the request, check the calendar, book the slot if it is free, and send a confirmation. Which design fits best?

options.text: A fixed workflow, since the steps and their order are known ahead
An agent, since a model choosing each step is always more reliable
An agent, since any feature that uses a model should be an agent
An agent, since it can skip the calendar check when a slot looks free

items.stem: A program always runs search_manuals on the student's question, pastes the top three passages into a prompt, and calls the model once to write the answer. How should you describe this system?

options.text: An agent, because the model writes the final answer in its own words
An agent, because the program uses a search tool to find the passages
A workflow, because a person reads each answer before the student does
A workflow, because the code fixes the steps and the model only writes

items.stem: Suppose a fixed workflow makes exactly 2 model calls per request, while an agent doing the same job averages 5 model calls per request. Assume every call costs the same. Over 200 requests, how many more model calls does the agent make than the workflow?
In one sentence, what must be true about a task's steps for an agent to be worth its extra cost over a fixed workflow?
Your team has a small model budget. In one sentence, why can you predict a fixed workflow's cost per request before running it, but not an agent's?
